title: Ryan Murphy’s Sanded-Down Version of “The Shards”
excerpt: The director’s adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s metafictional thriller-slash-gay-awakening story is a “Glee”-ified version of its source material, Leo Lasdun writes.
content_html:
Before the often controversial interview podcast and the many Twitter outbursts, before the precocious splash of “Less Than Zero” and the scandal of “American Psycho,” Bret Ellis—the writerly “Easton” still silent—was a student at the expensive Buckley School in Los Angeles. As a teen-ager, Ellis did drugs, saw R-rated movies, engaged in clandestine sexual affairs, and generally misbehaved, taking full advantage of the autonomy that well-off children were apparently granted in the early nineteen-eighties. That freedom is the backdrop of Ellis’s elegant autofictional 2023 novel “The Shards,” a thrilling reimagining of his adolescence that has now been transformed into a TV show by Ryan Murphy.

The novel’s drama springs from the arrival of a mysterious new student named Robert Mallory during senior year of high school. A fictionalized Bret Ellis and his friends are the popular kids, atop a social hierarchy that should, at this point, be set in stone; Robert’s addition to the mix makes Bret nervous. At the same time, Bret, who is gay and desperate to keep it secret, is immediately drawn to Robert. “The boy aroused something primal in me,” he recalls of their first encounter, at a screening of “The Shining.” Robert soon becomes an object of fantasy and fixation. Working off a few vague details, Bret begins to imagine a link between Robert and a serial killer known as the Trawler, who has been abducting and torturing young women around Los Angeles. When one of the Buckley seniors (a boy whom Bret has secretly been having sex with) goes missing, and is eventually found beaten and mutilated, Bret suspects that Robert is the killer.

Is he? In the novel, Robert is a shifty, slippery presence. Since we see him only through Bret’s eyes, it’s often unclear what about him is real and what is a projection of Bret’s protean desire. At “The Shining,” Bret lustily describes Robert’s head of blond hair. Later, his hair is brown. Sometimes we get a glimpse of Robert as a normal, affable teen before Bret’s narration once again assures us he’s a dangerous psychopath.

Bret has a girlfriend, Debbie Schaffer, but he also has sexual relationships with at least two of his male classmates. His feelings for these boys are described with a soul-baring softness, especially striking for its divergence from Ellis’s usual ruthless unsentimentality. On the other hand, Bret’s feelings for Robert lead him to take increasingly extreme measures, including stalking and, eventually, catastrophic violence. The intensity of his sexuality warps his mind, while the mandate of secrecy feeds his paranoia. The result, to borrow a phrase from Patrick Bateman, the serial killer in “American Psycho,” is that Bret feels “lethal, on the verge of frenzy.”

Equally lethal are Bret’s writerly aspirations. His ability to spin stories about the Trawler means that he is destabilized by the crimes in a way that his classmates aren’t. The achievement of the book is that Ellis (the real one) encases us in Bret (the character)’s obsessively narrativizing consciousness, so that his feverish pursuit of the “truth” rubs off on us. We, too, become fixated on whether small details might reveal Robert to be a murderer. Like Bret, we are eager to uncover the dark secrets of Robert’s past, but as the book goes on we are also creepingly aware that Bret might be more interested in a good story than he is in reality.

Murphy’s adaptation is a somewhat different product. Preserved from Ellis’s novel, and generally well-rendered, are the basic conceits and settings: a rich, secretly gay high-school senior named Bret Ellis is part of a friend group that integrates (or resists integrating) the newcomer Robert Mallory, all the while circled by news of the Trawler. Bret is played by Igby Rigney, whose distant, sneery monotone recalls the voice of the real-life Ellis. The rest of the cast, which includes Kaia Gerber and Homer Gere (the children of the eighties supermodel Cindy Crawford and the actor Richard Gere, respectively), is serviceable and occasionally great, but Rigney is the standout, and his presence or absence, from scene to scene, is starkly felt. The series is gorgeously shot, full of perfectly appointed eighties interiors, and has a soundtrack—Blondie, Fleetwood Mac, Rick James, and the Beach Boys—that evidently cost a fortune.

Ryan Murphy claims that he’s always “worshipped” Ellis’s work, and, indeed, one can imagine why the creator of “Glee,” a show about the agonies and the ecstasies of high-school drama, might find the adolescent milieu of “The Shards” compelling. But where “Glee” is a sentimental artifice, a snow-globe world in which teen-age angst and melodrama are of planetary importance, Ellis’s vision of teen-agers, as painted in “Less Than Zero,” his icy début, is numb, droll, sadistic, and alienated. In 2011, Ellis tweeted, “I like the idea of ‘Glee’ but why is it that every time I watch an episode I feel like I’ve stepped into a puddle of HIV?” In his own manner, Ellis may have summed up the disparity between his and Murphy’s sensibilities perfectly. As a novel, “The Shards” is an ambitious metafictional thriller-slash-gay-awakening story, and although, unlike “Less Than Zero,” it’s plot-forward and emotionally intense, Murphy’s attempt to adapt it has, to some degree, amounted to a “Glee”-ification.

Maximalist drama is Murphy’s signature style, and, to that end, he makes several stagy alterations to the novel’s subplots. One of Bret’s primary love interests, Ryan Vaughn, with whom he shares a tender weekend in the novel, is condemned, in the show, to a silly B plot involving (straight) porn and implausible blackmail. There’s a televised dance-off host’s short-lived and pointless baby-mama drama, and the addition of a bizarre kidnapping farce that, despite Ivy Wolk’s expressive and funny performance as its victim, morphs into a lame homecoming-queen makeover story before just being dropped. Perhaps most radical is the show’s portrayal of Bret’s relationship with Terry Schaffer, the father of Bret’s girlfriend, Debbie. In both the novel and the show, Terry is a famous movie producer who, though only nominally closeted, is still married to Debbie’s mother. At first, he comes across as a kind of quasi-predator—flirty and a little gross, but basically harmless. Then Terry takes an interest in Bret. From his daughter, he’s heard about Bret’s novel in progress, also called “Less Than Zero.” He wants to buy Bret lunch, to pick his brain, to encourage him to develop the novel into a screenplay. Then, Terry wants quid-pro-quo sex. In the show, Terry, played by Wes Bentley, is a cartoon creep, wearing a villainous grin as he instigates his sexual encounter with Bret. (We don’t see it; instead, much of the explicit passage from the novel is read verbatim by Rigney, in his flat voice-over.) The big departure comes in the show’s depiction of the aftermath: “I didn’t understand adult things, I just thought I did,” Bret reflects. “I’ve learned through time that many young people make the same mistake.”

This very appropriate, reasonable analysis is quite different from Ellis’s take on the scene in the novel. The business with Terry, Bret says there, “hadn’t bothered me in any substantial way.” In the book’s arc, this lands as a chilling dismissal, and a reminder of the magnitude of Bret’s increasingly psychotic concern over Robert Mallory and the Trawler, and his detachment from his own life. By contrast, Murphy fashions the moment into a statement on trauma, with Bret’s reflections about his youthful naïveté mirroring some of the language of the #MeToo movement. Regardless of the inherent morality of the situation (or if you even believe book-Bret is as unbothered as he claims), the turn is predictable and deflating.

“I didn’t care that Ronald Reagan had been elected president last November,” Bret muses in the novel. “This meant absolutely nothing to me at seventeen and politics have stayed that way for the rest of my life.” This little addendum—that politics mean nothing to the Bret Easton Ellis of 2023—is eminently untrue, as anyone who has listened to his podcast, which often turns to political commentary, will attest. There, Ellis seems, in fact, to have an irresistible negative attraction to politics. Perhaps he does find the whole thing uninteresting—and, on some level, even disgusting—but he can’t stay away. He worries about what he sees as the meddling of left-wing politics in the arts and entertainment (“Ideology trumps aesthetics,” he frequently complains), and the intensity of his claims of neutrality and aloofness belies what are obviously deep, genuine feelings about the political moment. In an interview with the writer Luke Goebel, the subject of the upcoming Los Angeles mayoral election came up. Ellis exclaimed, “The right is fucked, the left is fucked,” and went on, “If you live in L.A. and you’re voting for Karen Bass, or anybody else, you’re a nut case!” It’s clear from the rest of the conversation, and from numerous other statements he’s made—and from his 2019 essay collection, “White”—that “or anybody else” was a concession to his left-leaning guest: Ellis preferred the Republican candidate Spencer Pratt, who ultimately lost in the primary.

But “The Shards” is, indeed, something of a political void. There is vanishingly little connecting the novel to the real-life happenings of the eighties. (The most promising candidate for political analysis in the book comes in the form of the Terry Schaffer drama, which might be cast as a denouncement of “victim narratives,” something that Ellis has said that he hates.) This presents a bit of a problem for Murphy, for whom the prepackaged spectacle of political incident has become almost a prerequisite for entertaining television. His dramatizations “The People v. O. J. Simpson” and “Impeachment” (on the Monica Lewinsky scandal) are, arguably, his best works. In both cases, Murphy resists direct commentary, instead using politics as a set piece to make meaning and Shakespearean entertainment out of the players themselves. “The People” leverages the racial tensions surrounding the O.J. case as a dramatic engine, rather than a moral focus. At the heart of “Impeachment” are Lewinsky’s fateful friendship with Linda Tripp, and Bill and Hillary Clinton’s marriage.

With “The Shards,” Murphy doesn’t have as globally significant a set of events to work with. He uses the Trawler and the serial-killer narrative instead. Like the racial fracas of “The People” or the actual impeachment of “Impeachment,” the threat of the Trawler moves the story along, creating gravity and urgency. This is effective enough—we take the Trawler seriously, as a threat—but it also causes a tonal unevenness, and, ultimately, the show is caught in a kind of no man’s land, too schlocky to be menacing and too concerned with the grimness of its events to be a pure excess trip. Unlike in “The People” or “Impeachment,” the character material in “The Shards” doesn’t match the show’s alleged stakes. It’s too campy, too silly, too “Glee.” Ellis’s style isn’t universally beloved, but a character in one of his books probably wouldn’t employ the phrase “spooky season” to refer to October, or—ham-fisting the famous Joan Didion line—proclaim “I was . . . telling myself a story in order to live.”

Murphy obviously wasn’t interested in making a direct adaptation of Ellis’s novel, and most of the time it’s unclear what, exactly, he did want to do with the material. This is not, in any meaningful sense, a show about a teen-ager’s gay awakening, or the fraught management of such a secret; nor is it about the destructive and violent feelings that can accompany creative ambition. (In some ways, “Euphoria” is a better adaptation of “The Shards,” with its competing moral narratives and depictions of the often annihilating power of adolescent sexuality.) At times, Murphy’s show gestures at these themes, but not with any real conviction, and by the end of the series nothing much has been said.

A subject that Ellis likes to discuss on his podcast is how the New Hollywood era of the seventies came to an end with the flop of “Heaven’s Gate,” in early 1981, the same year that “The Shards” takes place. Ellis has an endearing, boyish fondness for the films of the New Hollywood (“Carrie,” “The Deer Hunter,” and “Days of Heaven” are regularly cited), their moral ambiguity and their often gloomy endings. In some sense, “The Shards” is a processing of Ellis’s transition into adulthood, as the cinematic landscape of his childhood died. “It was as if another world was announcing itself, painting the one we had all safely taken for granted into a darker color,” he writes. These lines refer to Robert Mallory’s arrival and the ensuing madness, but they could just as easily refer to the collapse of the Hollywood of Ellis’s youth. In the eighties, cinema would gravitate toward clear messages and sleek blockbusters, many of them action movies. Ellis is at odds with the linear, conformist optimism that defined that era—in 1991, with “American Psycho,” he created a whole serial killer out of his alienation—and in “The Shards” we again find him rejecting those clean, straightforward narratives, constantly hole-poking his own stories and revelling in the unresolved. I can’t help imagining a New Hollywood treatment of “The Shards”—one that incorporates the book’s strange inscrutability, its simultaneous resistance to and obsession with truth, its airy, suspenseful slowness. One that acknowledges the conundrum at the core of the book, and a prevailing force in Ellis’s work: We want to know what really happened. We’ll never know what really happened. ♦

blocks.html_en: Murphy’s adaptation is a somewhat different product. Preserved from Ellis’s novel, and generally well-rendered, are the basic conceits and settings: a rich, secretly gay high-school senior named Bret Ellis is part of a friend group that integrates (or resists integrating) the newcomer Robert Mallory, all the while circled by news of the Trawler. Bret is played by Igby Rigney, whose distant, sneery monotone recalls the voice of the real-life Ellis. The rest of the cast, which includes Kaia Gerber and Homer Gere (the children of the eighties supermodel Cindy Crawford and the actor Richard Gere, respectively), is serviceable and occasionally great, but Rigney is the standout, and his presence or absence, from scene to scene, is starkly felt. The series is gorgeously shot, full of perfectly appointed eighties interiors, and has a soundtrack—Blondie, Fleetwood Mac, Rick James, and the Beach Boys—that evidently cost a fortune.

blocks.html_en: Ryan Murphy claims that he’s always “worshipped” Ellis’s work, and, indeed, one can imagine why the creator of “Glee,” a show about the agonies and the ecstasies of high-school drama, might find the adolescent milieu of “The Shards” compelling. But where “Glee” is a sentimental artifice, a snow-globe world in which teen-age angst and melodrama are of planetary importance, Ellis’s vision of teen-agers, as painted in “Less Than Zero,” his icy début, is numb, droll, sadistic, and alienated. In 2011, Ellis tweeted, “I like the idea of ‘Glee’ but why is it that every time I watch an episode I feel like I’ve stepped into a puddle of HIV?” In his own manner, Ellis may have summed up the disparity between his and Murphy’s sensibilities perfectly. As a novel, “The Shards” is an ambitious metafictional thriller-slash-gay-awakening story, and although, unlike “Less Than Zero,” it’s plot-forward and emotionally intense, Murphy’s attempt to adapt it has, to some degree, amounted to a “Glee”-ification.

blocks.html_en: Maximalist drama is Murphy’s signature style, and, to that end, he makes several stagy alterations to the novel’s subplots. One of Bret’s primary love interests, Ryan Vaughn, with whom he shares a tender weekend in the novel, is condemned, in the show, to a silly B plot involving (straight) porn and implausible blackmail. There’s a televised dance-off host’s short-lived and pointless baby-mama drama, and the addition of a bizarre kidnapping farce that, despite Ivy Wolk’s expressive and funny performance as its victim, morphs into a lame homecoming-queen makeover story before just being dropped. Perhaps most radical is the show’s portrayal of Bret’s relationship with Terry Schaffer, the father of Bret’s girlfriend, Debbie. In both the novel and the show, Terry is a famous movie producer who, though only nominally closeted, is still married to Debbie’s mother. At first, he comes across as a kind of quasi-predator—flirty and a little gross, but basically harmless. Then Terry takes an interest in Bret. From his daughter, he’s heard about Bret’s novel in progress, also called “Less Than Zero.” He wants to buy Bret lunch, to pick his brain, to encourage him to develop the novel into a screenplay. Then, Terry wants quid-pro-quo sex. In the show, Terry, played by Wes Bentley, is a cartoon creep, wearing a villainous grin as he instigates his sexual encounter with Bret. (We don’t see it; instead, much of the explicit passage from the novel is read verbatim by Rigney, in his flat voice-over.) The big departure comes in the show’s depiction of the aftermath: “I didn’t understand adult things, I just thought I did,” Bret reflects. “I’ve learned through time that many young people make the same mistake.”

blocks.html_en: This very appropriate, reasonable analysis is quite different from Ellis’s take on the scene in the novel. The business with Terry, Bret says there, “hadn’t bothered me in any substantial way.” In the book’s arc, this lands as a chilling dismissal, and a reminder of the magnitude of Bret’s increasingly psychotic concern over Robert Mallory and the Trawler, and his detachment from his own life. blocks.html_en: “I didn’t care that Ronald Reagan had been elected president last November,” Bret muses in the novel. “This meant absolutely nothing to me at seventeen and politics have stayed that way for the rest of my life.” This little addendum—that politics mean nothing to the Bret Easton Ellis of 2023—is eminently untrue, as anyone who has listened to his podcast, which often turns to political commentary, will attest. There, Ellis seems, in fact, to have an irresistible negative attraction to politics. Perhaps he does find the whole thing uninteresting—and, on some level, even disgusting—but he can’t stay away. He worries about what he sees as the meddling of left-wing politics in the arts and entertainment (“Ideology trumps aesthetics,” he frequently complains), and the intensity of his claims of neutrality and aloofness belies what are obviously deep, genuine feelings about the political moment. In an interview with the writer Luke Goebel, the subject of the upcoming Los Angeles mayoral election came up. Ellis exclaimed, “The right is fucked, the left is fucked,” and went on, “If you live in L.A. and you’re voting for Karen Bass, or anybody else, you’re a nut case!” It’s clear from the rest of the conversation, and from numerous other statements he’s made—and from his 2019 essay collection, “White”—that “or anybody else” was a concession to his left-leaning guest: Ellis preferred the Republican candidate Spencer Pratt, who ultimately lost in the primary.

Like the racial fracas of “The People” or the actual impeachment of “Impeachment,” the threat of the Trawler moves the story along, creating gravity and urgency. blocks.html_en: Murphy obviously wasn’t interested in making a direct adaptation of Ellis’s novel, and most of the time it’s unclear what, exactly, he did want to do with the material. This is not, in any meaningful sense, a show about a teen-ager’s gay awakening, or the fraught management of such a secret; nor is it about the destructive and violent feelings that can accompany creative ambition. blocks.html_en: A subject that Ellis likes to discuss on his podcast is how the New Hollywood era of the seventies came to an end with the flop of “Heaven’s Gate,” in early 1981, the same year that “The Shards” takes place. Ellis has an endearing, boyish fondness for the films of the New Hollywood (“Carrie,” “The Deer Hunter,” and “Days of Heaven” are regularly cited), their moral ambiguity and their often gloomy endings. In some sense, “The Shards” is a processing of Ellis’s transition into adulthood, as the cinematic landscape of his childhood died. “It was as if another world was announcing itself, painting the one we had all safely taken for granted into a darker color,” he writes. These lines refer to Robert Mallory’s arrival and the ensuing madness, but they could just as easily refer to the collapse of the Hollywood of Ellis’s youth. In the eighties, cinema would gravitate toward clear messages and sleek blockbusters, many of them action movies. Ellis is at odds with the linear, conformist optimism that defined that era—in 1991, with “American Psycho,” he created a whole serial killer out of his alienation—and in “The Shards” we again find him rejecting those clean, straightforward narratives, constantly hole-poking his own stories and revelling in the unresolved. I can’t help imagining a New Hollywood treatment of “The Shards”—one that incorporates the book’s strange inscrutability, its simultaneous resistance to and obsession with truth, its airy, suspenseful slowness. One that acknowledges the conundrum at the core of the book, and a prevailing force in Ellis’s work: We want to know what really happened. We’ll never know what really happened. ♦

content_html_zh:
在经常引起争议的采访播客和推特上的多次爆发之前，在《不到零》的早熟轰动和《美国精神病人》的丑闻之前，布雷特·埃利斯——仍然保持沉默的作家“伊斯顿”——是洛杉矶昂​​贵的巴克利学校的一名学生。 十几岁的时候，埃利斯吸毒、看限制级电影、从事秘密性行为，并且行为不端，充分利用了十九世纪八十年代初期富裕孩子显然被授予的自主权。 这种自由是埃利斯 2023 年优雅的自传小说《碎片》的背景，这部小说对他的青春期进行了激动人心的重新想象，现已由瑞恩·墨菲改编成电视剧。

这部小说的戏剧性源于高中高年级时一位名叫罗伯特·马洛里的神秘新生的到来。 虚构的布雷特·埃利斯和他的朋友们是受欢迎的孩子，处于社会等级制度的顶端，在这一点上，这个等级制度应该是一成不变的；罗伯特的加入让布雷特感到紧张。 与此同时，身为同性恋且极力保守秘密的布雷特立即被罗伯特所吸引。 “这个男孩唤起了我内心深处的某种原始感觉，”他回忆起他们在《闪灵》放映时的第一次相遇。 罗伯特很快就成为幻想和迷恋的对象。 通过一些模糊的细节，布雷特开始想象罗伯特和一个名为“拖网渔船”的连环杀手之间的联系，该杀手一直在洛杉矶各地绑架和折磨年轻女性。 当巴克利的一名高年级学生（布雷特秘密与之发生性关系的男孩）失踪并最终被发现遭到殴打和肢解时，布雷特怀疑罗伯特就是凶手。

他是吗？ 在小说中，罗伯特是一个狡猾、狡猾的人。 由于我们只能通过布雷特的眼睛看到他，所以常常不清楚他的哪些部分是真实的，哪些是布雷特多变的欲望的投射。 在《闪灵》中，布雷特热情地描述了罗伯特的金发。 后来，他的头发变成了棕色。 有时我们会瞥见罗伯特是一个正常、和蔼可亲的青少年，然后布雷特的叙述再次向我们保证他是一个危险的精神病患者。

布雷特有一个女朋友黛比·谢弗，但他还与至少两名男同学发生了性关系。 他对这些男孩的感情被描述为一种赤裸裸的温柔，尤其引人注目的是它与埃利斯一贯的冷酷无情的不同。 另一方面，布雷特对罗伯特的感情导致他采取越来越极端的措施，包括跟踪，并最终采取灾难性的暴力。 他强烈的性欲扭曲了他的思想，而保密的要求则助长了他的偏执狂。 借用《美国精神病人》中连环杀手帕特里克·贝特曼的一句话，结果是布雷特感到“致命，处于疯狂的边缘”。

同样致命的是布雷特的作家抱负。 他编造有关拖网渔船故事的能力意味着他因犯罪行为而变得不稳定，而他的同学则不然。 这本书的成就在于，埃利斯（真实的人）将我们包裹在布雷特（角色）痴迷的叙事意识中，从而使他对“真相”的狂热追求感染了我们。 我们也开始关注小细节是否可能揭示罗伯特是凶手。 和布雷特一样，我们渴望揭开罗伯特过去的黑暗秘密，但随着书的继续，我们也逐渐意识到布雷特可能对好故事比他对现实更感兴趣。

墨菲的改编是一个有些不同的产品。 埃利斯的小说保留了基本的构思和背景，而且总体上呈现得很好：一个名叫布雷特·埃利斯的富有的、秘密同性恋的高中生是一个朋友团体的成员，这个朋友团体融入（或拒绝融入）新来者罗伯特·马洛里，而他一直被拖网渔船的新闻所包围。 布雷特由伊格比·里格尼 (Igby Rigney) 饰演，他冷漠、冷笑的单调声音让人想起现实生活中埃利斯的声音。 其余演员，包括凯亚·格伯和霍默·基尔（分别是八十年代超模辛迪·克劳馥和演员理查·基尔的孩子），都很有用，有时也很出色，但里格尼是最出色的，从一个场景到另一个场景，他的出现或缺席都让人感觉很明显。 该剧拍摄精美，充满了八十年代完美的内饰，并且有一个配乐——《金发女郎》、《弗利特伍德麦克》、《里克·詹姆斯》和《海滩男孩》——显然花费了一大笔钱。

瑞安·墨菲声称他一直“崇拜”埃利斯的作品，事实上，人们可以想象为什么《欢乐合唱团》（一部讲述高中戏剧的痛苦和狂喜的节目）的创作者可能会发现《碎片》的青少年环境引人注目。 但《欢乐合唱团》是一种感伤的诡计，是一个雪球世界，其中青少年的焦虑和情节剧具有全球重要性，而埃利斯在他冰冷的处女作《不到零》中所描绘的青少年形象是麻木的、滑稽的、虐待狂的和疏远的。 2011年，埃利斯在推特上写道：“我喜欢《欢乐合唱团》的想法，但为什么每次我看一集我都感觉自己踏入了艾滋病毒的深渊？” 埃利斯也许以他自己的方式完美地总结了他和墨菲的情感差异。 作为一部小说，《碎片》是一部雄心勃勃的元小说惊悚片，同性恋觉醒的故事，尽管与《不到零》不同，它的情节前卫且情感强烈，但墨菲对其进行的改编尝试在某种程度上相当于“欢乐合唱团”。

极繁主义戏剧是墨菲的标志性风格，为此，他对小说的次要情节进行了一些做作的修改。 布雷特的主要恋人之一瑞安·沃恩（Ryan Vaughn）在小说中与他度过了一个温柔的周末，在剧中，他被谴责为涉及（直接）色情和难以置信的勒索的愚蠢 B 情节。 其中有一场电视舞会主持人短命且毫无意义的婴儿妈妈戏剧，还增加了一场离奇的绑架闹剧，尽管艾维·沃尔克作为受害者表现得富有表现力和有趣，但在被丢弃之前却演变成一个蹩脚的返校节女王改头换面的故事。 也许最激进的是该剧对布雷特与特里·谢弗（布雷特女友黛比的父亲）关系的描绘。 在小说和电视剧中，特里都是一位著名的电影制片人，虽然名义上只出柜，但仍然与黛比的母亲结婚。 起初，他给人的印象是一种准掠夺者——轻浮，有点粗俗，但基本上是无害的。 然后特里对布雷特产生了兴趣。 他从女儿那里听说了布雷特正在创作的小说，也叫《小于零》。 他想请布雷特吃午餐，听取他的意见，鼓励他将小说改编成剧本。 然后，特里想要交换性行为。 在剧中，由韦斯·本特利 (Wes Bentley) 饰演的特里 (Terry) 是一个卡通怪人，在煽动与布雷特 (Bret) 发生性关系时，他脸上带着邪恶的笑容。 （我们没有看到它；相反，小说中的大部分明确段落都是里格尼在他平淡的画外音中逐字朗读的。） 最大的不同在于该剧对后果的描述：“我不明白成人的事情，我只是认为我明白，”布雷特反思道。 “随着时间的推移，我了解到很多年轻人都会犯同样的错误。”

这种非常恰当、合理的分析与埃利斯对小说中场景的看法截然不同。 布雷特在那里说，与特里的事“并没有对我造成任何实质性的困扰。” 在这本书的弧线中，这是一种令人不寒而栗的解雇，提醒人们布雷特对罗伯特·马洛里和拖网渔船日益疯狂的担忧，以及他对自己生活的脱离。 相比之下，墨菲将这一时刻塑造成关于创伤的声明，布雷特对自己年轻时天真的反思反映了#MeToo运动的一些语言。 不管这种情况的内在道德如何（或者如果你甚至相信书布雷特像他声称的那样无忧无虑），这种转变是可以预见的并且令人泄气。

“我不在乎罗纳德·里根去年 11 月当选总统，”布雷特在小说中沉思道。 “这对十七岁的我来说绝对没有任何意义，政治在我的余生中一直如此。” 这个小小的附录——政治对于 2023 年的布雷特·伊斯顿·埃利斯来说毫无意义——是非常不真实的，任何听过他的播客（经常转向政治评论）的人都会证明这一点。 事实上，埃利斯似乎对政治有着不可抗拒的负面吸引力。 也许他确实觉得整件事无趣——在某种程度上，甚至令人厌恶——但他无法置身事外。 他担心他所认为的左翼政治对艺术和娱乐的干涉（他经常抱怨“意识形态胜过美学”），而他对中立和冷漠的强烈主张掩盖了对政治时刻明显深刻、真实的感受。 在接受作家卢克·戈贝尔的采访时，谈到了即将举行的洛杉矶市长选举的话题。 埃利斯惊呼道：“右边完蛋了，左边也完蛋了，”然后继续说，“如果你住在洛杉矶。 如果你投票给凯伦·巴斯或其他任何人，你就是个疯子！” 从谈话的其余部分以及他所做的许多其他声明以及他 2019 年的散文集《怀特》中可以清楚地看出，“或任何其他人”是对他的左倾客人的让步：埃利斯更喜欢共和党候选人斯宾塞·普拉特，后者最终在初选中失败。

但《碎片》确实是一种政治真空。 小说与八十年代的现实生活中几乎没有什么联系。 （书中最有希望进行政治分析的候选人是特里·谢弗戏剧，该剧可能会被视为对“受害者叙事”的谴责，而埃利斯曾说过他讨厌这种叙事。） 这给墨菲带来了一些问题，对他来说，预先包装好的政治事件奇观几乎已经成为娱乐电视的先决条件。 他的戏剧《人民诉。 这。 J。 辛普森》和《弹劾》（关于莫妮卡·莱温斯基丑闻）可以说是他最好的作品。 在这两种情况下，墨菲都拒绝直接评论，而是将政治作为一种固定手段，让球员本身变得有意义和莎士比亚式的娱乐。 《人民》利用了围绕 O.J. 的种族紧张局势。 案件作为戏剧引擎，而不是道德焦点。 “弹劾”的核心是莱温斯基与琳达·特里普的命运般的友谊，以及比尔和希拉里·克林顿的婚姻。

在《碎片》中，墨菲没有需要处理的一系列具有全球意义的事件。 他用拖网渔船和连环杀手的叙述来代替。 就像《人民》中的种族骚乱或《弹劾》中的实际弹劾一样，拖网渔船的威胁推动了故事的发展，创造了严肃性和紧迫性。 这足够有效——我们认真地对待拖网渔船，将其视为一种威胁——但它也导致了基调的不平衡，最终，这部剧陷入了一种无人区，太粗俗而不能具有威胁性，也太关注其事件的严峻性，不能成为纯粹的多余旅行。 与《人民》或《弹劾》不同，《碎片》中的人物素材与该剧所谓的赌注不符。 这太做作了，太傻了，太“欢乐合唱团”了。 埃利斯的风格并不受到普遍喜爱，但他的一本书中的人物可能不会用“幽灵季节”这个词来指代十月，或者——用火腿拳头著名的琼·迪迪恩台词——宣称“我是……” 为了活下去，给自己讲一个故事。”

墨菲显然对直接改编埃利斯的小说不感兴趣，而且大多数时候都不清楚他到底想用这些材料做什么。 从任何有意义的意义上来说，这并不是一部关于青少年同性恋觉醒的剧，也不是关于如何处理这样一个秘密的剧；而是一部关于青少年同性恋觉醒的剧。它也不是关于伴随创造性野心而来的破坏性和暴力情感。 （在某些方面，《幸福感》是《碎片》的更好改编版，它具有相互竞争的道德叙事和对青少年性欲的毁灭性力量的描述。） 有时，墨菲的表演对这些主题做出了姿态，但没有任何真正的信念，并且在该系列结束时什么也没说。

埃利斯喜欢在播客中讨论的一个主题是，七十年代的新好莱坞时代如何随着 1981 年初《天堂之门》的失败而结束，同年《碎片》上映。 埃利斯对新好莱坞电影有着一种可爱而孩子气的喜爱（《魔女嘉莉》、《猎鹿人》和《天堂之日》经常被引用）、它们的道德模糊性和往往令人沮丧的结局。 从某种意义上说，《碎片》是埃利斯向成年过渡的过程，因为他童年的电影景观已经消失。 “就好像另一个世界正在宣告自己，将我们都认为理所当然的世界涂成更深的颜色，”他写道。 这些台词指的是罗伯特·马洛里的到来和随之而来的疯狂，但它们也可以很容易地指代埃利斯年轻时好莱坞的崩溃。 八十年代，电影倾向于清晰的信息和时尚的大片，其中许多是动作片。 埃利斯与那个时代所定义的线性、顺从的乐观主义格格不入——1991年，在《美国精神病人》中，他出于疏离感创造了一个完整的连环杀手——而在《碎片》中，我们再次发现他拒绝那些干净、直截了当的叙述，不断地戳自己的故事，陶醉于未解决的问题。 我情不自禁地想象着新好莱坞对《碎片》的处理方式——融合了这本书奇怪的神秘性、对真相的同时抵制和痴迷，以及它轻快、悬疑的缓慢。 它承认了本书的核心难题，也是埃利斯作品中的主导力量：我们想知道到底发生了什么。 我们永远不会知道到底发生了什么。 ❖
